eras.title: Key Topic 1: Queen, Government and Religion, 1558–69
Key Topic 2: Challenges to Elizabeth at Home and Abroad, 1569–88
Key Topic 3: Elizabethan Society in the Age of Exploration, 1558–88

milestones.title: Accession of the Virgin Queen: Legitimacy, Debt & Privy Council
milestones.specTag: KT 1.1 • Society, Government & Problems of Accession (1558)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did doubts over legitimacy, gender, marriage, and Crown debt threaten Elizabeth in 1558?
milestones.imageCaption: Queen Elizabeth I in her cloth-of-gold coronation robes holding the orb and sceptre after ascending the throne in November 1558.
milestones.catalyst: Aged twenty-five in November 1558, **the Virgin Queen** inherited **£300,000** in Crown debt (borrowing in Antwerp at 14% interest) alongside patriarchal prejudice over her **gender** and Catholic doubts over her **legitimacy** as Anne Boleyn's daughter.
milestones.turningPoint: Fluent in six languages and resolute in character, Elizabeth immediately appointed **Sir William Cecil** Principal Secretary, streamlined a 19-man **Privy Council**, and used royal **patronage** to bind rival nobles to her court.
milestones.impact: Established firm administrative grip without surrendering her royal prerogative over **marriage**, though refusing to wed left England without a Protestant child heir while unpaid **Justices of the Peace** enforced local order.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Domestic fiscal and dynastic fragility was compounded immediately by military humiliation across the Channel and a rival Catholic claimant to the north.

keyTerms.definition: Image cultivated by unmarried Elizabeth I turning her refusal to take a foreign or factional husband into a symbol of devotion to England.
Lawful right to inherit the Crown; devout Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate because the Pope never annulled Henry VIII's first marriage.
Elite 19-man executive council managed by Elizabeth through grants of Crown offices, land leases, and commercial monopolies.

milestones.title: Loss of Calais, The Auld Alliance & Early Foreign Encirclement
milestones.specTag: KT 1.1 • Challenges from Abroad: France, Scotland & Spain
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did losing Calais and the Franco-Scottish Auld Alliance endanger England in 1558?
milestones.imageCaption: Sixteenth-century engraving of the Old Bourse at Antwerp, where the indebted Tudor Crown borrowed money to fund coastal defence.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Strategic encirclement of England in 1558 by Catholic France, French-garrisoned Scotland, and Habsburg Spain.
milestones.catalyst: Mary I's costly war alongside Spain had lost **Calais**—England's last continental foothold—in January 1558, while France stationed veteran troops in Scotland under the **Auld Alliance**.
milestones.turningPoint: Catholic claimant **Mary, Queen of Scots**, married to French Dauphin **Francis II**, quartered the English royal arms with her own; Elizabeth wisely signed the **Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis (1559)** and backed Scottish Protestants in 1560.
milestones.impact: Avoided a ruinous two-front Catholic crusade when England lacked a standing army or cash, though French civil war after 1562 and Elizabeth's failed Le Havre venture ended hopes of regaining Calais.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To prevent foreign Catholic powers exploiting unrest inside England, Elizabeth summoned Parliament in early 1559 to settle the nation's bitter religious divide.

keyTerms.definition: Humiliating surrender of England's last French port under Mary I, leaving the southern English coast exposed across the Channel.
Traditional military alliance between Catholic France and Scotland that placed French troops along England's northern border.

milestones.title: Elizabeth’s Religious Settlement: Supremacy, Uniformity & Injunctions
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2 • Features of the 1559 Settlement of Religion
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Elizabeth's 1559 Religious Settlement balance Protestant doctrine with traditional form?
milestones.imageCaption: Printed title page of the 1559 Elizabethan Book of Common Prayer establishing a single English pattern of parish worship.
milestones.catalyst: England was split between conservative Catholic earls and northern gentry, 26 Marian bishops in the House of Lords, and returning **Marian exiles** demanding a Calvinist church.
milestones.turningPoint: Parliament passed the **Act of Supremacy** (making Elizabeth **Supreme Governor** via a clergy oath) and **Act of Uniformity** (English **Book of Common Prayer**, Ornaments Rubric, and **12d recusancy fine**), backed by **57 Royal Injunctions**.
milestones.impact: Created an inclusive Protestant *via media* ('middle way'): ambiguous communion wording and traditional vestments calmed moderate **Church Papists** while securing Protestant royal control over the Church.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Passing statutes at Westminster was only half the task; royal commissioners now toured every diocese while strict Puritans attacked remaining Catholic ornaments.

keyTerms.definition: Statute severing ties with Rome and naming Elizabeth 'Supreme Governor' rather than 'Supreme Head' to calm Catholic and male critics.
Law enforcing the 1559 English Book of Common Prayer across every parish and fining Sunday absentees (recusants) one shilling (12d).
Fifty-seven practical instructions ordering English parish Bibles and preaching royal supremacy while banning pilgrimages and 'feigned' miracles.

milestones.title: Enforcing the Settlement, Church Role & The Puritan Crucifix Challenge
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2–1.3 • Role of the Church of England & Early Puritan Challenge
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did visitations enforce order—and why did Puritans challenge royal crucifixes?
milestones.imageCaption: Hand-coloured frontispiece of the Elizabethan Bishops' Bible depicting Queen Elizabeth I flanked by Justice and Mercy.
milestones.catalyst: While **Church courts** policed village morals and pulpits preached royal obedience, zealous returning **Puritans** condemned organs, holy days, and silver **crucifixes** as popish superstition.
milestones.turningPoint: In autumn 1559, 125 royal commissioners conducted **visitations** (only **~400 of 8,000 clergy** refused the oath); when Protestant bishops threatened resignation over Elizabeth's Royal Chapel crucifix, she removed it, and Puritans lost by **one vote** at the **1563 Convocation**.
milestones.impact: Demonstrated overwhelming parish compliance across rural England while showing Elizabeth would yield tactically on a chapel ornament yet block any clerical vote to alter her statutory settlement.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Alongside parish pulpits, Protestant humanism and rising commercial wealth fuelled rapid growth in town grammar schools and class-stratified Elizabethan leisure.

keyTerms.definition: Official diocesan inspections ensuring clergy swore the Oath of Supremacy, used the English Prayer Book, and removed superstitious images.
Ecclesiastical courts enforcing everyday parish morality by prosecuting slander, adultery, heresy, sabbath-breaking, and disputed wills.
Early 1560s clash when Puritan bishops forced Elizabeth to remove her Royal Chapel crucifix where rural parishes lacked replacement clergy.

milestones.title: Humanist Education, Endowed Grammar Schools & Social Pastimes
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Education in the Home & Schools; Sport & Pastimes
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Elizabethan schooling and leisure reflect both humanist growth and social rank?
milestones.imageCaption: Sixteenth-century English woodcut of a Tudor town grammar schoolroom with schoolmaster, birch rod, and Latin scholars.
milestones.catalyst: Protestant emphasis on Bible reading, humanist scholarship, and expanding urban trade encouraged wealthy benefactors and guilds to endow **42 grammar schools in the 1560s** and **30 more in the 1570s**.
milestones.turningPoint: Nobility hired private tutors; gentry and merchant boys studied Latin and Greek at **grammar schools** (after **petty schools**) before **Oxford, Cambridge**, or the Inns of Court, while leisure split noble **hunting, hawking, and real tennis** from village **folk football** and shared **bear-baiting**.
milestones.impact: Male literacy rose to roughly **30%** (and female literacy to **10%**) by the 1580s, yet schooling reinforced the **Great Chain of Being**: farm labourers' children worked from age six and women remained barred from universities.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Educated Protestant clergy remained divided over church dress, bringing Elizabeth and Archbishop Parker into open confrontation with London Puritans in 1566.

keyTerms.definition: Fee-paying town schools for gentry, merchant, and yeoman boys aged 10–14 teaching classical Latin, Greek, rhetoric, and obedience.
Elementary home-based schools teaching basic hornbook reading, arithmetic, or needlework before apprenticeships or grammar school.
Rank-divided leisure pitting noble deer-hunting, hawking, and fencing against rough parish football and cross-class Southwark bear-baiting.

milestones.title: Archbishop Parker’s Book of Advertisements & The Vestments Controversy
milestones.specTag: KT 1.3 • Scope & Impact of the Puritan Challenge
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Archbishop Parker defeat Puritan defiance over clerical vestments in 1566?
milestones.imageCaption: Matthew Parker, moderate Protestant Archbishop of Canterbury appointed by Elizabeth I to enforce clerical uniformity.
milestones.catalyst: Puritan ministers refused to wear the white linen **surplice** and square cap required by the 1559 Ornaments Rubric, condemning special priestly dress as *'rags of Rome'*.
milestones.turningPoint: Ordered by Elizabeth to enforce uniformity, Archbishop **Matthew Parker** issued his March 1566 **Book of Advertisements**, exhibited approved garments at Lambeth Palace, and deprived **37 non-conforming London Puritan priests** of their livings.
milestones.impact: Exposed the limits of the Puritan challenge: lacking noble leadership, foreign backing, or any Protestant alternative to Elizabeth, most Puritans conformed rather than lose their pulpits.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While domestic Puritan resistance subsided after 1566, militant Counter-Reformation Catholicism surged dangerously across the Narrow Sea in the Spanish Netherlands.

keyTerms.definition: Mid-1560s refusal by zealous Puritan clergy to wear the prescribed white linen surplice during parish worship.
Archbishop Matthew Parker's rulebook enforcing uniform clerical dress and depriving 37 defiant London ministers.

milestones.title: The Duke of Alba in Flanders & Seizure of the Genoese Loan
milestones.specTag: KT 1.3 • Catholic Challenge from the Papacy & Foreign Powers
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Alba's Spanish army in Flanders and the Genoese Loan spark a trade crisis?
milestones.imageCaption: Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, 3rd Duke of Alba, commander of King Philip II's Spanish army sent to crush Dutch Protestantism in 1567.
milestones.catalyst: Pope Pius V's **Counter-Reformation** hardened Catholic attitudes from 1566, William Allen founded the **Douai** seminary (1568), and King **Philip II** sent the **Duke of Alba** with **10,000 veteran Spanish troops** into the Netherlands (1567).
milestones.turningPoint: In **November 1568**, five Spanish ships carrying **£85,000** in gold bullion (**the Genoese Loan** bound to pay Alba's army) sheltered in English ports; advised by Cecil, Elizabeth legally impounded the gold for the English Crown.
milestones.impact: Starved Alba's army in Flanders of vital pay right across the Channel, but provoked Spain's retaliatory **Antwerp trade embargo**, halting English woollen cloth exports and souring Anglo-Spanish relations.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Just months before the Genoese Loan clash, Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots fled across the Solway Firth into Cumbria—handing English Catholics a rival figurehead inside England.

keyTerms.definition: The Duke of Alba's notorious 'Council of Blood' in the Spanish Netherlands that executed thousands of Dutch Protestants.
£85,000 in Italian bank bullion bound for Alba's army in Antwerp that Elizabeth impounded when Spanish ships sheltered in English ports.
Catholic college in Flanders founded by William Allen to train missionary priests to keep Catholicism alive in England.

milestones.title: Flight of Mary, Queen of Scots & The York Casket Letters Inquiry
milestones.specTag: KT 1.4 • Mary Stuart's Claim & Relations with Elizabeth (1568–69)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why was Mary, Queen of Scots' arrival in May 1568 an impossible dilemma for Elizabeth?
milestones.imageCaption: Miniature portrait of Mary, Queen of Scots, legitimate Catholic great-granddaughter of Henry VII held in English captivity from 1568.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Lord Darnley's murder, Mary's escape from Lochleven, flight into Cumbria (May 1568), and English castle captivity.
milestones.catalyst: After **Lord Darnley**'s 1567 murder at Kirk o' Field and Mary's scandalous marriage to Bothwell, Protestant Scottish lords forced her abdication for infant **James VI**; escaping **Lochleven**, Mary fled into England in **May 1568**.
milestones.turningPoint: Trapped because restoring, releasing, or executing an anointed cousin all carried grave risks, Elizabeth held the **York Inquiry (Oct 1568–Jan 1569)** over the **Casket Letters**, delivering a **'not proven'** verdict to keep Mary under house arrest.
milestones.impact: Preserved friendly Protestant Regency rule in Scotland without trying a fellow queen, yet keeping Catholic **heir presumptive** Mary inside England immediately inspired a court plot to wed her to the **Duke of Norfolk**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While court intrigue brewed around Mary in 1569, Flemish mapmaking and English shipyard breakthroughs were simultaneously laying the technical foundations of oceanic power.

keyTerms.definition: Mary Stuart's strong dynastic status as Henry VII's great-granddaughter while unmarried Elizabeth lacked a child of her own.
Eight French letters and love sonnets produced by Regent Moray at York as alleged proof Mary plotted Lord Darnley's murder.

milestones.title: Mercator’s 1569 World Map, Navigational Science & Race-Built Galleons
milestones.specTag: KT 3.3 • New Technology on Ships, Navigation & Trade Expansion
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Mercator maps, astrolabes, and race-built galleons transform English voyages?
milestones.imageCaption: Gerardus Mercator's 1569 navigational world map projection plotting compass bearings across parallel latitude and longitude grids.
milestones.catalyst: Antwerp's cloth-trade collapse (from 1568) forced London merchants into joint-stock ventures like the **Muscovy**, **Eastland**, and **Levant** Companies while captains needed safer open-ocean navigation.
milestones.turningPoint: Flemish cartographer **Gerardus Mercator** published his **1569 projection map** alongside brass **astrolabes**, **quadrants**, and **log-and-line** speed gauges, while Naval Treasurer **Sir John Hawkins** designed fast, low **race-built galleons** armed with long-range **culverins**.
milestones.impact: Combined square and triangular **lateen sails** with heavy broadside firepower and ocean endurance—enabling both global exploration (Drake, Frobisher) and England's decisive 1588 naval superiority over Spain.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Back in northern England in autumn 1569, Elizabeth's arrest of the Duke of Norfolk triggered the reign's only major domestic armed rebellion.

keyTerms.definition: Navigational world map placing latitude and longitude on a grid so sailors could plot straight constant-compass courses across oceans.
Precision brass instruments measuring the angle of the midday sun or Polaris to calculate north-south latitude at sea.
Sleek, lower-hulled English warships pioneered by John Hawkins combining Atlantic stability, agile lateen sails, and heavy culverin gun decks.

milestones.title: The Revolt of the Northern Earls: Durham Mass & Royal Retribution
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Reasons for & Significance of the Northern Revolt (1569–70)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the 1569 Revolt of the Northern Earls break out—and why did it fail?
milestones.imageCaption: Thomas Percy, 7th Earl of Northumberland, who rose with the Earl of Westmorland in November 1569 to restore Catholicism.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: March of the Northern Earls through Durham Cathedral, Hartlepool, and Barnard Castle before royal suppression (Nov–Dec 1569).
milestones.catalyst: Catholic earls **Northumberland** and **Westmorland** resented losing northern power and income under Protestant Bishop **James Pilkington** and feared arrest when the **Norfolk marriage plot** collapsed in September 1569.
milestones.turningPoint: In **November 1569**, **4,600 rebels** tore up the English Bible in **Durham Cathedral** and celebrated Latin Mass; when Alba sent no Spanish troops to Hartlepool and Elizabeth moved Mary to Coventry, royal troops crushed the rising and executed **450 rebels**.
milestones.impact: Proved most English Catholics and northern gentry remained loyal to the Tudor Crown, yet prompted harsher treason statutes, confiscated rebel estates, and a reconstructed Protestant **Council of the North** under Huntingdon.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Only weeks after the northern rising collapsed, Pope Pius V fatally escalated religious conflict by excommunicating Elizabeth from Rome.

keyTerms.definition: November 1569 Catholic rebellion by Northumberland and Westmorland aiming to free Mary Stuart, restore Latin Mass, and oust Cecil.
Royal administrative council in York reorganised under Protestant President Henry Hastings, Earl of Huntingdon, after the 1569 rebellion.

milestones.title: Regnans in Excelsis (1570), The Ridolfi Plot & Execution of Norfolk
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Papal Excommunication & Catholic Conspiracy (1570–72)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the 1570 Papal Bull and 1571 Ridolfi Plot transform the Catholic threat?
milestones.imageCaption: Pope Pius V's February 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis excommunicating Elizabeth I and releasing Catholics from allegiance.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Catholic noble strongholds, Mary Stuart's prison transfers, and foreign invasion schemes against Elizabethan England.
milestones.catalyst: **Pope Pius V**'s February 1570 bull ***Regnans in Excelsis*** excommunicated Elizabeth as a heretic and ordered English Catholics to depose her, turning religious loyalty into suspected treason (**1571 Treasons Act**).
milestones.turningPoint: In **1571**, Italian banker **Roberto Ridolfi** plotted with **Philip II**, Alba (**10,000 Spanish troops**), Mary Stuart, and the **Duke of Norfolk** to overthrow Elizabeth; Cecil and Walsingham intercepted coded letters and executed Norfolk in **June 1572**.
milestones.impact: Revealed Spain's willingness to back Elizabeth's overthrow and ended leniency toward Catholic plotters, though Elizabeth still resisted parliamentary calls to execute anointed monarch Mary Stuart.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Fear that rural poverty and wandering vagrants could fuel further rebellion prompted Parliament in 1572 to pass sweeping national poor legislation.

keyTerms.definition: Papal bull excommunicating Elizabeth I and absolving English Catholics of their oaths of loyalty to the Crown.
Foiled international conspiracy by banker Roberto Ridolfi to land 10,000 Spanish troops, depose Elizabeth, and wed Mary Stuart to Norfolk.

milestones.title: Population Growth, Sheep Enclosure & The 1572 Vagabonds Act
milestones.specTag: KT 3.2 • Increase in Poverty & Vagabondage; Early Policy
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did poverty and vagabondage rise—and how did the 1572 Act respond?
milestones.imageCaption: Woodcut from Thomas Harman's A Caveat for Common Cursitors (1567) warning magistrates against sturdy beggars and vagabonds.
milestones.catalyst: England's population surged **35% (from 3m to 4m)** alongside bad harvests, coin-debasement inflation, **rack-renting**, and **enclosure** for lucrative **sheep farming** (needing a tenth the workers of arable grain), fuelling widespread **vagabondage**.
milestones.turningPoint: Guided by Thomas Harman's warnings against **'sturdy beggars'**, the **1572 Vagabonds Act** combined a **compulsory weekly poor rate** for the **impotent poor** with harsh punishment: unlicensed vagrants were whipped and **bored through the ear** (hanging for repeat offences).
milestones.impact: Established national compulsory local taxation for deserving parish poor for the first time, while reflecting gentry terror (without a police force) that masterless vagrants spread crime, plague, and sedition.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Recurring cloth-trade slumps in the mid-1570s soon convinced MPs that many able-bodied poor genuinely lacked jobs rather than choosing idleness.

keyTerms.definition: Hedging open village fields and common land into private sheep pastures for wool exports, evicting rural farm labourers.
Wandering without a settled parish home or master; feared by Tudor JPs as a cause of crime, disease, and rebellion.
Tudor distinction between deserving orphans, elderly, and sick unable to work versus physically capable ('sturdy') unemployed adults.

milestones.title: Changing Attitudes: The 1576 Poor Relief Act & Houses of Correction
milestones.specTag: KT 3.2 • Changing Attitudes & Policies Towards the Poor
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the 1576 Poor Relief Act mark a turning point in attitudes toward unemployment?
milestones.imageCaption: Sixteenth-century English woodcut depicting an able-bodied vagrant ('Upright Man') during the Elizabethan poor-law debates.
milestones.catalyst: Antwerp cloth embargoes and poor harvests (1573–77) proved that thousands of **able-bodied poor** wanted honest work yet could not find employment through no fault of their own.
milestones.turningPoint: Parliament passed the **1576 Poor Relief Act** (*Act for Setting the Poor on Work*), ordering Justices of the Peace to supply **raw wool, flax, hemp, and iron** so the unemployed could earn wages, while sending refusers to county **Bridewells** (Houses of Correction).
milestones.impact: Marked a constructive shift from pure physical deterrence to state-organised employment relief—forming with the 1563 and 1572 Acts a national framework of parish responsibility that endured throughout Elizabeth's reign.
milestones.bridgeToNext: That same year—helped by the 1572 Vagabonds Act licensing noble acting troupes—Elizabethan popular culture blossomed in London's first permanent playhouse.

keyTerms.definition: Statute requiring towns and parishes to provide raw wool, hemp, and flax to employ able-bodied poor unable to find work.
County institutions established under the 1576 Act where persistent vagrants who refused parish work faced strict hard labour.

milestones.title: Burbage’s ‘The Theatre’ (1576), Penny Groundlings & Puritan Opposition
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Growth of Secular Drama & The Theatre
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did purpose-built London playhouses thrive across all classes despite Puritan anger?
milestones.imageCaption: Authentic Elizabethan wooden hornbook used to teach foundational literacy in petty schools as print and playgoing expanded.
milestones.catalyst: Because the **1572 Vagabonds Act** required touring actors to hold a nobleman's licence, professional companies like **Leicester's Men** and **the Queen's Men (1583)** formed as mystery plays were suppressed.
milestones.turningPoint: In **1576**, actor **James Burbage** opened England's first purpose-built playhouse, **'The Theatre'**, in Shoreditch outside City of London jurisdiction, followed by **The Curtain (1577)** and **The Rose (1587)**, drawing 2,000 spectators per show.
milestones.impact: United Elizabethan society under one roof—poor **groundlings** stood in the open yard for **1d** while gentry sat in covered **2d–3d galleries**—despite **Puritan** and City aldermen protests over plague, crime, and idleness.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Just one year after 'The Theatre' opened in London, Francis Drake sailed secretly from Plymouth to challenge Spain's Pacific empire around the globe.

keyTerms.definition: England's first permanent purpose-built playhouse erected by James Burbage in Shoreditch in 1576.
Ordinary labourers and apprentices who paid one penny to stand in the open pit around the thrust stage.
Licensed royal acting company formed under Walsingham's patronage, touring Protestant patriotic plays across England.

milestones.title: Sir Francis Drake’s Circumnavigation of the Globe in the Golden Hind
milestones.specTag: KT 3.3 & KT 2.2 • Reasons for & Significance of Drake's Voyage
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why was Drake's 1577–80 circumnavigation so significant for English wealth and sea power?
milestones.imageCaption: Sixteenth-century engraving of Francis Drake's flagship Golden Hind capturing Spain's Pacific treasure ship Cacafuego in March 1579.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Global route of Francis Drake's circumnavigation (1577–80) via the Strait of Magellan, Peru, Nova Albion, and the Moluccas.
milestones.catalyst: Seeking to avenge Spain's **1568 San Juan de Ulúa** ambush, break Philip II's Pacific trade monopoly, and win royal plunder, **Francis Drake** sailed from Plymouth in December 1577 with secret backing from Elizabeth, Walsingham, and Leicester.
milestones.turningPoint: Navigating the stormy **Strait of Magellan** in his flagship ***Golden Hind***, Drake raided Chile and Peru, captured the treasure ship ***Cacafuego*** (£140,000), claimed **Nova Albion** in North America, traded Moluccan cloves, and returned in **Sept 1580 with £400,000**.
milestones.impact: Delivered investors a **4,700% profit**, cleared England's entire Crown debt from Elizabeth's share, proved English mariners could circle the globe, and inspired **Raleigh's Virginia** plans while infuriating Madrid.
milestones.bridgeToNext: When King Philip II—newly strengthened by annexing Portugal in 1580—demanded Drake's head as a pirate, Elizabeth staged a brazen public reply on the Thames.

keyTerms.definition: Drake's renamed flagship (formerly Pelican) that captured Spain's rich Pacific silver galleon Cacafuego off Ecuador in March 1579.
North American Pacific coast ('New England', likely California) welcomed by Miwok people and claimed by Drake for Queen Elizabeth.

milestones.title: Anglo-Spanish Rivalry & Elizabeth’s Defiant Knighting of Drake at Deptford
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Political, Religious & Commercial Rivalry with Spain
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did publicly knighting Francis Drake at Deptford in April 1581 infuriate Philip II?
milestones.imageCaption: Contemporary portrait engraving by Jodocus Hondius of Sir Francis Drake, knighted by Elizabeth I aboard the Golden Hind in April 1581.
milestones.catalyst: Tensions over **privateering**, English indirect loans to ** Dutch Protestant rebels** after the **1576 Spanish Fury** in Antwerp, and Philip II's **1580 annexation of Portugal** brought Madrid and London close to confrontation.
milestones.turningPoint: Defying Spanish Ambassador Mendoza's demand to punish 'El Draque', Elizabeth boarded the ***Golden Hind*** at **Deptford** in **April 1581** and had a French envoy dub **Sir Francis Drake** a knight while she funded the French Duke of Alençon in Flanders.
milestones.impact: Publicly endorsed privateering raids against Spain's New World empire, signalled an anti-Spanish alignment with France, and convinced **Philip II** that Elizabeth was an open enemy of Habsburg Catholic power.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Determined to remove England's Protestant queen, Spanish ambassador Mendoza and French Catholic nobles financed a secret invasion plot around Mary Stuart in 1583.

keyTerms.definition: Crown-licensed raids by private armed English vessels against Spanish treasure ships and ports, yielding royal profit with deniability.
Mutinous sack of Antwerp by unpaid Spanish troops that briefly united all 17 Dutch provinces under the Pacification of Ghent.

milestones.title: The Throckmorton Plot, Expulsion of Mendoza & The Bond of Association
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Jesuit Mission, Throckmorton Plot & Spy Network
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did uncovering the 1583 Throckmorton Plot sever ties with Spain and trap Mary Stuart?
milestones.imageCaption: Sir Francis Walsingham, Principal Secretary and spymaster whose surveillance network broke the 1583 Throckmorton and 1586 Babington plots.
milestones.catalyst: Underground **Jesuit missionaries** (like **Edmund Campion**, executed 1581) prompted **£20 monthly recusancy fines**, driving desperate Catholic conspirators to seek Franco-Spanish military intervention.
milestones.turningPoint: In **November 1583**, **Sir Francis Walsingham** arrested courier **Francis Throckmorton**, exposing a Spanish-funded plan for Mary's cousin, the French **Duke of Guise**, to invade Sussex; Elizabeth expelled Ambassador **Mendoza** and Cecil drafted the **1584 Bond of Association**.
milestones.impact: Severed formal diplomatic relations between England and Spain (Mendoza was never replaced) and created the legal mechanism (made statute in **1585**) under which Mary Stuart would face death if anyone plotted on her behalf.
milestones.bridgeToNext: As Anglo-Spanish diplomacy collapsed in 1584, Sir Walter Raleigh secured a royal patent to plant an English Protestant base in North America to rival Spain.

keyTerms.definition: Foiled plan for French Catholic forces under the Duke of Guise—paid by Spain and backed by the Pope—to invade England and free Mary.
Pledge signed by nobles (enacted as statute in 1585) to execute anyone attempting or benefiting from Elizabeth's assassination.

milestones.title: Sir Walter Raleigh’s Patent & Failure of the First Roanoke Settlement
milestones.specTag: KT 3.4 • Causes & Failure of the First Virginia Settlement (1585–86)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Raleigh promote Virginia—and why did the 1585–86 Roanoke colony fail?
milestones.imageCaption: John White's 1585 watercolour of the Algonquian village of Secotan in Virginia showing Native maize fields and dwellings.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Roanoke Island, Ocracoke Inlet (where the Tiger grounded in June 1585), and Algonquian villages along coastal Virginia.
milestones.catalyst: Granted a **March 1584 royal patent** (and backed by Richard Hakluyt's *Discourse on Western Planting* plus 1584 envoy liaisons **Manteo and Wanchese**), **Sir Walter Raleigh** sought a North American base to raid Spanish silver ships, supply ship timber, and expand trade.
milestones.turningPoint: Sailing late in **April 1585** with **107 male colonists** (too many soldiers/gentlemen, too few farmers) under **Sir Richard Grenville** and **Ralph Lane**, flagship ***Tiger*** hit an Ocracoke sandbar ruining seed corn; famine and Lane's **June 1586 killing of Chief Wingina** forced evacuation with Drake.
milestones.impact: Highlighted how late departure, spoiled supplies, poor skill balance, and violent alienation of Algonquian hosts doomed England's first colony—though **Thomas Harriot** and **John White** mapped valuable American resources.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While Lane's colonists struggled on Roanoke in summer 1585, Protestant disaster in the Netherlands forced Elizabeth into open continental war with Spain.

keyTerms.definition: North American territory named for the Virgin Queen and Outer Banks island site of Raleigh's 1585 and 1587 colonial attempts.
Grounding of Grenville's flagship at Ocracoke Inlet that flooded the colonists' seed corn and forced reliance on Algonquian food.
Secotan Algonquian ruler who halted food trade during drought and was killed in Ralph Lane's pre-emptive June 1586 ambush.

milestones.title: The Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) & Robert Dudley’s Campaign in the Netherlands
milestones.specTag: KT 2.3 • Outbreak of War with Spain: Direct Intervention in Flanders
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Nonsuch trigger war with Spain—and why did Dudley's Dutch campaign struggle?
milestones.imageCaption: Sixteenth-century engraving of Nonsuch Palace in Surrey, where Elizabeth I signed the Anglo-Dutch alliance in August 1585.
milestones.catalyst: Following **William of Orange's July 1584 assassination**, the **Duke of Parma**'s rapid reconquest of Antwerp, and Spain's **December 1584 Treaty of Joinville** with French Catholics, Dutch collapse threatened England's Channel security.
milestones.turningPoint: Signing the **Treaty of Nonsuch (10 Aug 1585)**, Elizabeth garrisoned Flushing and Brielle and sent **7,400 troops** under **Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester**—who enraged Elizabeth by accepting **Governor-General** (Jan 1586) before suffering betrayals at **Deventer** and **Zutphen** (Jan 1587).
milestones.impact: Philip II treated Nonsuch as an open declaration of war and began building the **Enterprise of England** (Armada); although underfunded and distrusted after Stanley and Yorke defected, Dudley kept deep-water **Ostend** out of Parma's hands.
milestones.bridgeToNext: With England and Spain effectively at war in Flanders, Catholic plotters inside England launched one final conspiracy in summer 1586 to murder Elizabeth.

keyTerms.definition: Franco-Spanish Catholic alliance between Philip II and the French Catholic League that isolated Protestant England.
Anglo-Dutch alliance committing 7,400 English soldiers under Leicester to defend Dutch Protestants—triggering open war with Spain.
Dutch strongholds betrayed to Parma by Catholic English officers William Stanley and Rowland Yorke, wrecking Dutch trust in Leicester.

milestones.title: Walsingham’s Beer-Barrel Trap & The Babington Plot
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Walsingham's Spy Network & Entrapment of Mary Stuart
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Walsingham's double agents and codebreakers trap Babington and Mary in July 1586?
milestones.imageCaption: Deciphered Babington Plot postscript annotated by Walsingham's cryptographer Thomas Phelippes with a gallows mark in July 1586.
milestones.catalyst: Young Catholic gentleman **Anthony Babington** organised six conspirators to assassinate Elizabeth, free **Mary Stuart** from Chartley Hall, and welcome a **60,000-strong Franco-Spanish invasion**.
milestones.turningPoint: Walsingham's double agent **Gilbert Gifford** intercepted every coded letter smuggled inside **beer barrels**, while codebreaker **Thomas Phelippes** deciphered Mary's **17 July 1586** reply explicitly approving Elizabeth's *'dispatch'* (murder).
milestones.impact: Handed Walsingham incontrovertible written proof of Mary's treason under the **1585 Act for the Preservation of the Queen's Safety**; Babington and his fellow plotters were executed in September 1586 and Mary was convicted in October.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Despite Parliament's unanimous demand for Mary's death, Elizabeth agonised for four months before signing the fatal execution warrant in February 1587.

keyTerms.definition: Catholic conspiracy to murder Elizabeth and rescue Mary Stuart, monitored from start to finish by Walsingham's intelligence ring.
Double agent Gilbert Gifford's courier channel routing Mary's coded Chartley Hall letters directly to cryptographer Thomas Phelippes.

milestones.title: The Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots at Fotheringhay Castle
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Reasons for & Significance of Mary's Execution (1587)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why was the February 1587 execution of Mary, Queen of Scots a decisive turning point?
milestones.imageCaption: Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots inside the Great Hall of Fotheringhay Castle on 8 February 1587.
milestones.catalyst: Open war with Spain, repeated assassination plots, and Phelippes's deciphered Babington letter convinced Privy Councillors that Elizabeth's life remained in mortal peril while Mary lived.
milestones.turningPoint: After Elizabeth signed the warrant on 1 February 1587, Privy Councillors secretly dispatched it; on **8 February 1587** at **Fotheringhay Castle**, Mary Stuart went to the block wearing crimson Catholic martyr's petticoats.
milestones.impact: Permanently eliminated the domestic Catholic alternative monarch inside England without provoking war from her Protestant son **James VI** (kept loyal via a £4,000 pension), yet Mary bequeathed her English throne claim directly to **Philip II of Spain**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: With Philip II now claiming the English crown directly and assembling an invasion fleet in Spanish ports, Elizabeth unleashed Francis Drake on a pre-emptive strike.

keyTerms.definition: Northamptonshire fortress where Mary, Queen of Scots was tried in October 1586 and beheaded for high treason.
Anglo-Scottish alliance paying Protestant King James VI an annual £4,000 subsidy, ensuring Scotland did not avenge Mary's execution.

milestones.title: Drake’s Raid on Cadiz: ‘Singeing the King of Spain’s Beard’
milestones.specTag: KT 2.3 • Pre-Emptive Strike & Logistical Disruption of the Armada
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Drake's April 1587 raid on Cadiz weaken Spain's Armada before it sailed?
milestones.imageCaption: Sir Francis Drake's squadron bombarding and burning Spanish warships and stores inside Cadiz harbour in April 1587.
milestones.catalyst: Walsingham's intelligence network warned in early 1587 that **Philip II** was gathering warships and supplies across Iberian harbours to invade England following Nonsuch and Mary Stuart's execution.
milestones.turningPoint: On **19 April 1587**, **Sir Francis Drake** led 24 ships into **Cadiz**, burning **30 Spanish vessels**, before destroying seasoned oak **barrel staves** off Cape St Vincent and capturing the treasure carrack ***San Felipe*** (£108,000).
milestones.impact: Delayed the Spanish Armada by **twelve vital months** so England could fortify its coast, and forced Spain to pack food and water in leaky green-pine casks that rotted at sea during the 1588 campaign.
milestones.bridgeToNext: One month after Cadiz, Raleigh dispatched a second family colony to Virginia—only for the delayed Spanish Armada emergency to cut off their relief ships.

keyTerms.definition: Drake's nickname for his daring April 1587 raid on Cadiz destroying 30 ships and delaying Spain's Armada until 1588.
Seasoned oak cask timbers burned by Drake off Cape St Vincent, forcing Spain to use damp pine barrels that spoiled Armada provisions.

milestones.title: John White’s Second Roanoke Settlement & The ‘Lost Colony’
milestones.specTag: KT 3.4 • Second Attempted Colonisation of Virginia & Maritime War
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did John White's 1587 Roanoke settlement become the 'Lost Colony'?
milestones.imageCaption: Artist-governor John White's hand-drawn watercolour map of coastal Virginia and Roanoke Island.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Roanoke Island, Croatoan Island, and the Chesapeake Bay destination intended for John White's 1587 settlers.
milestones.catalyst: Learning from 1585's all-male military failure, **Raleigh** sent artist-governor **John White** in **May 1587** with **118 men, women, and children** promised 500-acre family farms on Chesapeake Bay.
milestones.turningPoint: Pilot Simon Fernandez landed them back on hostile **Roanoke** instead; after colonist George Howe was killed, White sailed home for urgent supplies in **August 1587**, but Elizabeth requisitioned **every seaworthy English ship in 1588** to fight the **Spanish Armada**.
milestones.impact: Cut off relief for three crucial years, leaving the **'Lost Colony'** vanished with only **'CROATOAN'** carved on a post—proving early English colonisation lacked Crown funding and survival skills while teaching vital lessons for later plantations.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Those requisitioned English ships gathered at Plymouth in July 1588 as Medina Sidonia's 130-ship Spanish Armada entered the English Channel.

keyTerms.definition: John White's 118-settler family colony at Roanoke stranded without supplies when Elizabeth held back all ships against the 1588 Armada.
Friendly Croatoan Algonquian ally named Lord of Roanoke in August 1587 to try to rebuild local Native diplomacy.

milestones.title: Defeat of the Spanish Armada: Calais Fireships, Gravelines & Tilbury
milestones.specTag: KT 2.4 • Spanish Invasion Plans, Key Events & Reasons for English Victory
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did England defeat Philip II's Spanish Armada in July–August 1588?
milestones.imageCaption: English race-built galleons firing close-range broadsides into scattered Spanish warships at the Battle of Gravelines, 8 August 1588.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Track of the 1588 Spanish Armada through the Channel, Calais fireships, Gravelines, and gale-swept wrecks off Scotland and Ireland.
milestones.catalyst: Philip II ordered the **Duke of Medina Sidonia**'s **130 ships** (30,000 men) to escort the **Duke of Parma**'s 27,000 Flanders troops across to Kent, yet Parma lacked a **deep-water port** and **Dutch flyboats** blockaded his shallow-canal barges.
milestones.turningPoint: Chased past Plymouth and the Isle of Wight to exposed **Calais Roads**, Spain's crescent was scattered by **eight midnight English fireships (7 Aug)**; on **8 August** at **Gravelines**, rapid English broadsides battered the fleet before **'Protestant Wind'** gales wrecked >25 anchorless ships off Scotland and Ireland.
milestones.impact: Only **67 Spanish ships** limped home; combined with Elizabeth's rousing **Tilbury speech (18 Aug 1588)**, victory secured Protestant England, preserved Dutch independence, and cemented Tudor royal authority and naval prestige.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Thirty years after ascending an indebted, divided throne in 1558, Elizabeth I emerged in 1588 with her Protestant settlement intact and England's oceanic future launched.

keyTerms.definition: Eight tar-and-gunpowder vessels drifted into Calais anchorage at midnight, panicking Spanish captains into cutting their main anchors.
Decisive nine-hour battle off Flanders where agile English race-built galleons fired three times faster than Spanish boarding ships.
Fierce gales driving Spain's battered fleet onto Scottish/Irish rocks while Elizabeth rallied troops at Tilbury ('heart and stomach of a king').
